blocks.h: Why is `prev` reset at each level?
p: The ordering rule applies within a level only, left to right. Resetting `prev = None` at the start of each level stops the last value of one level from being compared with the first of the next. Strictness (`<=` / `>=` as violations) forbids equal neighbours.

blocks.h: Why sell the highest values first, in groups?
p: Each sale yields the current maximum stock, so greedily selling the best available ball each time is optimal. Doing it one ball at a time would take `orders` steps (up to 10⁹). Selling whole levels at once, with arithmetic-series sums, handles huge orders in O(n log n). Checking the formula against a one-ball-at-a-time greedy on 200 random small inputs: True.

p: `'cabbba'` and `'abbccc'` are close:

blocks.h: Why these two conditions are enough
p: Operation 1 lets us arrange the letters in any order, so positions don't matter. Operation 2 swaps the roles of two letters, so it can give any frequency to any letter as long as the multiset of frequencies matches and the set of letters is the same. Hence the words are close exactly when both conditions hold. For example `'abc'` vs `'aab'` fails the letters check even though frequencies sorted `[1,1,1]` vs `[1,2]` also differ.

bullets: Time: O(n + k log k) where k ≤ 26.

1657.takeaway: Two strings are close iff they have the same letter set and the same multiset of letter frequencies.

Current total time of worker w

p: jobs `[1,2,4,7,8]` (sorted `[8, 7, 4, 2, 1]`), `k = 2` → 11. The recursion makes 26 calls to `go`. Complete assignments that improved the best:

blocks.h: Why do both pruning rules matter?
p: Without pruning the search tries k^n assignments. The bound `>= best` discards any partial assignment already as bad as the best known. The equal-load check removes mirrored duplicates: giving a job to either of two empty workers produces equivalent states. Together with processing large jobs first, they make the search fast for n ≤ 12.

bullets: Time: O(k^n) worst case, far less with pruning.

1723.takeaway: Backtracking with pruning: sort jobs descending, skip placements that can't beat the best, and skip workers with identical loads.

head: Code
What it does
When to reach for it
rows: Number of pairs with each product
Ways to choose 2 of the c pairs with the same product
Each choice of two pairs gives 8 ordered tuples
Swap within each pair (2·2) and swap the two pairs (2) = 8

blocks.h: Why does the count of pairs give the tuples?
p: A tuple (a, b, c, d) with a·b = c·d is two disjoint pairs {a, b} and {c, d} with the same product. All numbers are distinct, so two different pairs with the same product can't share an element (if they shared x, the other elements would be equal). Each unordered choice of two such pairs yields 8 ordered tuples, hence `8 * C(c, 2)` per product value.

bullets: Space: O(n²) for the product counter.

1726.takeaway: Group pairs by product; each choice of two pairs with the same product gives 8 ordered tuples.

blocks.h: Why does the crossing condition suffice?
p: A palindrome built from a subsequence of word1 followed by a subsequence of word2 has its first letter from word1 and its last from word2 (both non-empty). Those two letters form the outermost matching pair, which is exactly a pair (i, j) with i in word1 and j in word2 and s[i] == s[j]. p: orders `[[10,5,0],[15,2,1],[25,1,1],[30,4,0]]` ([price, amount, type]) → backlog total 6:

A buy order needs the lowest-priced sell, and a sell order needs the highest-priced buy. A min-heap of sells and a max-heap of buys give exactly those in O(log n). Matching consumes orders from the heap tops, so the match order follows the price priority described in the problem.

bullets: Time: O(n log n): every order is pushed and popped at most a constant number of times (partial fills re-push the remainder once per match).

1801.takeaway: Order book with two heaps: a min-heap of sells and a max-heap of buys; match while the best prices cross and push back remainders.

What it does

rows: The insertion goes into the shorter one
Count matching words from the front

The suffix must not overlap the matched prefix
Words already matched at the front can't be counted twice
Prefix + suffix cover all of the shorter sentence
Then the rest of the longer sentence is the inserted part

p: `'My name is Haley'` and `'My Haley'`: shorter = `['My', 'Haley']`, longer = `['My', 'name', 'is', 'Haley']`.

blocks.h: Why does matching front and back work?
p: Inserting a sentence at one position in the shorter sentence means the shorter sentence's words split into a prefix and a suffix that both appear in the longer sentence, at its start and end. So the shorter one is similar to the longer one exactly when its words can be covered by a matching prefix plus a matching suffix. The `j < len(a) - i` guard avoids double-counting words when prefix and suffix would overlap.

bullets: Space: O(n + m) for the word lists.

1813.takeaway: Compare words from both ends: the shorter sentence must be fully covered by a matching prefix plus a matching suffix.
